notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 13 from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Exodus 13 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Structure and Overview

Matthew Henry (via Precept Austin) divides the chapter into three parts:
1. Commands to Israel: to sanctify all firstborn (vv. 1–2), remember deliverance (vv. 3–4), keep unleavened bread (vv. 5–7), teach children (vv. 8–10), and set apart firstlings of cattle with explanation to children (vv. 11–16).
2. God’s care for Israel: choosing their way (vv. 17–18) and guiding them in it (vv. 20–22).
3. Their care of Joseph’s bones (v. 19).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-13-commentary

Precept Austin also notes the chapter can be outlined: vv. 1–2 (God to Moses – firstborn); vv. 3–10 (Moses to people – unleavened bread); vv. 11–16 (Moses to people – firstborn continued); vv. 17–22 (departure begins).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-13-commentary

---

### v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses"

The word “Then” connects to the events of Exodus 12:50–51: Israel had obeyed and the LORD brought them out. This instruction was given while Israel was at Succoth (Gill).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 2 — "Consecrate to Me every firstborn male … both of man and beast"

**Traditional reading (Gill):** “Sanctify” means to separate or devote to God’s service. Only males are meant — not females. The firstborn of clean animals were sacrificed; unclean animals and human firstborn were redeemed with money given to the priests. Applies only to Israelites, not Gentiles. “It is Mine” means God had a special claim on these firstborn because He spared them when Egypt’s firstborn were destroyed.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**Ellicott:** It was a “reasonable demand” that the existing firstborn spared by God should be set apart for His service. The extension to future firstborn was meant to perpetuate the memory of the deliverance. Redemption of firstborn sons naturally followed once the Levitical priesthood was established (Numbers 3:40‑51).
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

**David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Three reasons the firstborn belongs to God: (1) Israel itself was God’s firstborn (Ex 4:22); (2) the firstborn was thought to be the best, and the best belongs to God; (3) a perpetual reminder of when God redeemed Israel. “Consecrate” could mean either “sacrifice” or “consider as belonging to God” (Cole).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Precept Austin (multiple commentators):** The firstborn were “purchased with the blood of the blemish-free lamb.” God claims the best — J. Vernon McGee notes that the gods of Egypt had always claimed the firstborn, and now God claims Israel’s firstborn. Wiersbe adds that each time a firstborn male came into the world, the redemption ritual reminded Israel of God’s grace. God claims “the first and the best” from believers today.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-13-commentary

---

### v. 3 — "Remember this day … out of the house of slavery … nothing leavened shall be eaten"

**Gill:** “House of bondage” means “house of servants.” They were to remember the day (15th of Nisan) because it was by God’s mighty hand, not their own power, that they were freed. Gill sees a parallel to the Lord’s Supper: Christians remember redemption by Christ.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**Precept Austin:** The Septuagint translates “remember” with a present-tense imperative — continual, conscious effort to recall. This is directed to all the people. Believers likewise must continually remember their redemption by the blood of the Lamb.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-13-commentary

**Ellicott:** Remembrance was secured in four ways: (1) the month Abib beginning the ecclesiastical year; (2) the Passover; (3) seven days of unleavened bread; (4) the redemption of the firstborn and the questions it would provoke.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 4 — "Today, in the month of Abib, you are leaving"

**Ellicott:** Abib means “green ears of corn” or “greenness” — the month when wheat came into ear. It was a shifting month beginning with the full moon after the vernal equinox (roughly March–April). The name was later replaced by “Nisan” during the Babylonian captivity.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

**Gill:** The Syriac version renders it “month of flowers”; it was spring, a very fit time to travel. Jarchi noted God’s mercy in bringing them out at a season with neither extreme heat, nor cold, nor rain.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 5 — "When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites … you shall keep this service in this month"

**Gill:** This verse (with v. 11) suggests that the laws concerning unleavened bread and sanctifying the firstborn were not fully obligatory until Israel entered Canaan. However, they did keep Passover in the wilderness (Numbers 9:1), though unleavened bread is not mentioned there.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**Ellicott:** Kalisch concluded that only two Passovers were kept before entering Canaan — one by Moses at Sinai (Num 9:1–5) and one by Joshua at Gilgal (Josh 5:10–11).
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

**Bridgeway:** The five nations listed (out of seven — Girgashites and Perizzites omitted here) represent the inhabitants of the Promised Land.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-13.html (from search excerpt)

---

### vv. 6–7 — "Seven days … unleavened bread … seventh day a feast to the LORD"

**Guzik:** The purity of unleavened bread follows blood-deliverance at Passover — illustrating that we can only walk in purity after the blood-deliverance at the cross. Yet the week was not joyless; it began and ended with a feast.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Ellicott:** The seventh day (21st of Abib) was regarded by Jews as the anniversary of the Red Sea crossing.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 8 — "You are to explain to your son, ‘This is because of what the LORD did for me’"

**Gill:** Parents were to teach all their children — sons and daughters — the reason for eating unleavened bread: God’s swift deliverance left no time to leaven the dough.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**Precept Austin:** The emphasis is on transmitting the knowledge of redemption to the next generation. The deliverance was personal: “what the LORD did for me.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-13-commentary

---

### v. 9 — "A sign on your hand and a reminder on your forehead … the Law of the LORD is to be on your lips"

**Guzik (Enduring Word):** God wanted deliverance from Egypt constantly before their eyes. Jews later used this passage (with Deut 6:4–9; 11:13–21) to institute *phylacteries* (small boxes with Scripture worn on forehead and hand). Jesus later condemned the Pharisees’ abuse of this practice (Matt 23:5). However, the phrase “that the LORD’s law may be in your mouth” proves the language is metaphorical — you cannot put a phylactery box *in your mouth*.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Gill:** These are the words of an Israelite parent to a son: the feast would serve as a memory aid, like tying something on the hand or placing it before the eyes. The “law in your mouth” means being able to speak of God’s works and transmit the knowledge. “This cannot be taken literally.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**Ellicott:** The practice of wearing *tephillin* (phylacteries) is referred by Jews themselves to the time of the Exodus. A similar custom existed in Egypt (Wilkinson). Moses may have adopted an existing custom but purged it of superstition, substituting Scripture for magic charms. The injunctions in Deut 6:6–9 “seem to have been intended, and were certainly understood, literally.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

**Bridgeway:** The language is figurative. Later Jews took it literally and created phylacteries — small boxes containing Scripture texts worn on arm and forehead (see Matt 23:5).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-13.html (from search excerpt)

---

### v. 10 — "You shall keep this statute at the appointed time year after year"

**Gill:** The Hebrew reads “from days to days” — meaning either year after year, or that the feast was to be observed for the full seven days when the season arrived.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

---

### vv. 11–13 — Firstborn of livestock belong to the LORD; donkeys redeemed with a lamb; firstborn sons redeemed

**Gill:** “Set apart” (literally “cause to pass over”) means transferring from the owner’s use to the LORD’s. Only males are the LORD’s. The donkey (representing all unclean beasts) was to be redeemed with a lamb — the only acceptable substitute per Jewish canon. If not redeemed, its neck was to be broken (cut off with a butcher’s cleaver), so the owner had no profit. Human firstborn were redeemed with five shekels (Num 18:16). This shows humans are by nature unclean and need redemption by the blood of the Lamb.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**Ellicott:** The donkey is specifically mentioned because Israelites possessed donkeys (not horses). The ass was considered “Typhonian” in Egypt — associated with the evil god Set — hence unclean. Redeeming a donkey with a lamb was economically favourable to the owner (the lamb was worth less). Breaking the neck was a deterrent: it would be effective without needing enforcement.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

**Guzik:** “Set apart” translates a Hebrew phrase meaning “make them pass over” (i.e., by fire) — the same sinister phrase used of Ahaz sacrificing his son to Molech (2 Kings 16:3). But here, redemption replaces sacrifice for humans and unclean animals. A substitute was offered to redeem the firstborn from God. For animals, the substitute was a clean animal; for humans, money.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Bridgeway:** Clean animals were sacrificed; unclean animals were redeemed with a clean substitute; human sacrifice was forbidden — children were redeemed by payment of money.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-13.html (from search excerpt)

---

### vv. 14–15 — "When your son asks … ‘With a mighty hand the LORD brought us out … Pharaoh stubbornly refused … the LORD killed every firstborn’"

**Gill:** The son’s question (“What is this?”) would arise when he saw the separation of clean firstlings or the redemption of unclean ones and humans. The answer points to the LORD slaying all Egyptian firstborn — both man and beast — when Pharaoh stubbornly refused. Therefore clean firstborn males are sacrificed, and human firstborn sons are redeemed (for five shekels each). Gill describes the ongoing Jewish redemption ceremony: at thirty days old, a priest asks the mother if the child is her firstborn; the father pays gold and silver to redeem the child.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**John Piper (Desiring God):** Piper reflects on the bluntness of “the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt.” He notes that if he had been an Egyptian, his eldest son would have died. Piper emphasizes God’s absolute creator rights: “God does not owe anybody 70 years … It isn't murder when God takes the life of a person. It’s simply taking back what He gave in a time that He deems wise.” The application: “It is a comforting and sweet thing to say, ‘God is God.’”
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-providence-of-god-session-9

---

### v. 16 — "A sign on your hand and a symbol on your forehead"

**Gill:** Observing these laws about firstlings and redemption would serve as a memory token, like something tied on the hand or placed on the forehead — visible and constantly recalled.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

**Guzik:** The practice of dedicating the firstborn would be a reminder through ritual of God’s great work for Israel. Guzik notes the end-times Satanic counterfeit: the mark of the Beast on hand or forehead (Rev 13:16).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Ellicott:** The Hebrew word *totaphoth* (“frontlets”) and its Chaldee equivalent *tephillin* both mean “bands” or “circlets.” The injunctions here could be explained metaphorically, but those in Deut 6:6–9 were understood literally.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 17 — "God did not lead them … through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter"

**Guzik:** The coastal route (the *Via Maris*, “way of the sea”) was the shortest and most common route from Egypt to Canaan, but it was lined with Egyptian military outposts. God knew Israel was not spiritually ready for war: “Lest perhaps the people change their minds when they see war, and return to Egypt.” Application: God will never allow us to face more than we can bear (1 Cor 10:13). “He tempts not above what we are able” (Trapp).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Ellicott:** The route from Tanis along the coast through Pelusium to Gaza was about 200 miles — doable in a fortnight. The text anticipates the question: why not the short way? Answer: God knew they would face the warlike Philistines and might, if defeated, return to Egypt. Ellicott notes that the Philistines were already a strong, warlike people — they later gave their name to “Palestine.” After four centuries of slavery, Israel would have been an “ill match” for them.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 18 — "God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea … arrayed for battle"

**Guzik:** The “Red Sea” here refers not to the 100‑mile-wide expanse but to the western “finger” — the modern Gulf of Suez.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Ellicott:** “Harnessed” is a mistranslation. The Hebrew word does not mean “armoured.” It means “organised” or “in military order.” The Israelites could not have had armour before the Red Sea crossing (they later stripped the dead Egyptians). The word indicates an orderly departure, not a chaotic flight. This organisation had been developing during the year of conflict with Pharaoh (see Ex 4:29; 6:26; 12:3, 21, 51).
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 19 — "Moses took the bones of Joseph"

**Guzik:** Joseph had asked that his bones be taken from Egypt (Gen 50:25) because he knew Egypt was not Israel’s final resting place. His coffin remained above ground for about 400 years as a silent witness that God’s promise to bring Israel to Canaan would be fulfilled. Now it was being fulfilled.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Ellicott:** Joseph’s body had been embalmed in Egyptian fashion. He had ordered its transport to Canaan (Gen 50:25).
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

**Bridgeway (from search excerpt):** Moses carried Joseph’s bones in accordance with Joseph’s earlier request, expressing faith that one day his people would return to the Promised Land (cf. Heb 11:22).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-13.html

---

### v. 20 — "They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness"

**Ellicott:** The exact positions of Succoth and Etham are uncertain. Succoth may have been near Tel Dafneh (~15 miles from Tanis); Etham near modern Ismailia. “Etham” may mean “house of Tum” — pointing to a temple of the Egyptian sun-god. Brugsch’s identification of Etham with Egyptian *Khetam* is “highly improbable” because Hebrew *aleph* never replaces Egyptian *kh*.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

**Guzik:** “The exact location of Etham is unknown” (Kaiser).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

---

### v. 21 — "The LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud … and in a pillar of fire"

**Guzik:** The pillar of cloud by day and fire by night was a dramatic, constant assurance of God’s presence. The Hebrew word for “pillar” literally means “something standing” — more like a column. Adam Clarke calls it the *Shechinah* — the divine dwelling place and continual proof of God’s presence and protection. Psalm 105:39 and Psalm 84:11 are cross-references: God as “a sun and shield.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Ellicott:** The LORD moved in front of the host in a form resembling smoke by day and fire by night. When the pillar moved, the people moved; when it stopped, they encamped. It bore resemblance to fire-and-smoke signals used by ancient generals leading armies (Lepsius, Q. Curtius), but was “altogether of a miraculous and abnormal character.” The night journeys are mentioned again in Num 9:21.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

---

### v. 22 — "Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people"

**Guzik:** Despite this constant visible evidence of God’s presence, Israel would still doubt, rebel, and act as if God was distant — “a sobering reminder of human weakness in faith.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/

**Ellicott:** The cloud probably disappeared at Abel-shittim (Num 33:49). See also Ex 40:38; Num 9:16; 10:34.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Perspectives

### Phylacteries — Literal or Metaphorical? (vv. 9, 16)

This is the clearest point where Protestant traditions diverge:

- **Evangelical / figurative reading (Guzik, Gill, Bridgeway):** The language is pure metaphor. The phrase “that the law may be in your mouth” proves it cannot be literal — you cannot put a box in your mouth. Guzik calls it “metaphorical language, not a literal directive.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-13/
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/13.htm

- **Anglican / Ellicott (historically informed):** The injunctions in Exodus 13 *could* be explained metaphorically, but those in Deuteronomy 6:6–9 “seem to have been intended, and were certainly understood, literally.” The practice of *tephillin* is traced by Jews to the Exodus itself. A similar custom existed in Egypt; Moses may have adopted it, purged of superstition, to turn a current practice to good use.
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/13.htm

### Reformed / God’s Sovereign Ownership of Life (v. 15)

**John Piper (Desiring God / Reformed Baptist):** Emphasises God’s absolute creator rights. “God does not owe anybody 70 years … It isn’t murder when God takes the life of a person. It’s simply taking back what He gave.” The killing of Egypt’s firstborn is not an ethical problem when one starts with God’s sovereignty rather than human rights.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-providence-of-god-session-9

### Redemption by Substitution (v. 13)

**Pulpit Commentary Homiletics (from search excerpt on biblehub.com):** The law for redeeming the donkey with a lamb illustrates that “redemption is by substitution.” The donkey (unclean, unfit for altar) must be redeemed by a lamb — or die. This teaches: “unredeemed life must die.” Jesus fulfils this under both aspects — substitution of His holy life for our sinful ones (Heb 9:26–28) and His life given as “a ransom for many” (Matt 20:28; 1 Tim 2:6). “Redeemed life belongs to God” (vv. 1, 12, 15).
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/13.htm

### Constable (Evangelical / Dallas Seminary)

Constable notes that “every” refers to firstborn males only (clear from the Hebrew word and context of vv. 12–13). The dedication was to occur after entering the land, but “God took the Levites for His special possession in place of the first-born” at Sinai (Num 3:12–13), so this dedication never took place as originally commanded. Instead, Israelites circumcised their sons and observed Passover when they entered (Josh 5:4–7).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-13.html (from search excerpt)

## Other Views

### Catholic / Orthodox

I was unable to retrieve content from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search and fetch limits. No specific Catholic or Orthodox readings can be reported here.

### Modern Scholarship

I was unable to fetch pages from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the tool limits. However, the Bridgeway Commentary (from search excerpt) notes that the “Red Sea” (literally “Sea of Reeds”) was not the 200‑kilometre-wide sea we call the Red Sea today, but probably an extension of the Gulf of Suez — a large shallow expanse of water near the line of the present-day Suez Canal.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-13.html
